recent_posts.title: Fly.io ❤️ Kamal
recent_posts.summary: The post discusses the author's experience with using Kamal for deployment, including setting up the machines, daily usage, and the underlying technology. It also mentions the author's plans to continue using Kamal alongside Fly.io.

recent_posts.title: Execute Third Party Code in a Rails App
recent_posts.summary: This post discusses the problem of executing third-party code in a Rails app and how Fly.io provides a solution with their Machines API. It explains the risks associated with executing arbitrary code and the need for a safe environment. The post also provides an example of how to integrate sandboxes and ensure the security and isolation of the executed code.

recent_posts.title: Rails on Docker without Docker
recent_posts.summary: Rails developers can deploy to production without needing to learn Docker or Linux systems administration thanks to Fly.io. The dockerfile-rails gem automates the process of creating Dockerfiles for Rails apps. Kamal, another deployment tool, can be used with Fly.io, but it is not necessary since Fly.io handles load balancing, Docker builds, and restarts.

recent_posts.title: 8 Turbo 8 "Gotchas"
recent_posts.summary: Turbo 8 offers new features like page morphs and it's important to be aware of certain 'gotchas' when updating existing Rails Turbo apps. Scroll properties, autofocus attribute, and preserving form inputs are some key points to keep in mind. Caching and Turbo Rails meta tags are also discussed.

recent_posts.title: Turbo 8 in 8 minutes
recent_posts.summary: Turbo 8 simplifies Rails development by minimizing the need for manual coding of turbo frames and turbo stream responses. It allows for live-updating Rails applications by automatically applying changes to pages without reloading the entire page.

recent_posts.title: SQLite Persistence Canary
recent_posts.summary: SQLite Persistence Canary: How do you properly educate developers their rebuild-the-world-from-scratch deployments could destroy their production data? In 2021 Rails introduced a way of displaying a warning message in the logs: You are running SQLite in production, this is generally not recommended. This was a very reasonable approach in 2021.

recent_posts.title: Audience of One

Follow the steps to build a Rails application that streams output to the browser. Discover the precautions taken to ensure security when allowing random people to provide commands to be executed on a server.

recent_posts.title: Accommodating Safari Users
recent_posts.summary: The article discusses the problem with Safari users in Rails applications and the limitations of import maps. It introduces esbuild as a tool to perform necessary changes for Safari users and provides a custom rake task for using esbuild. The esbuild.rake script runs esbuild to minify and target older browsers. The installation process for esbuild is also explained. By using the esbuild script, Rails applications can provide interactivity to all users.

recent_posts.title: Better Rails Forms with Superform
recent_posts.summary: Build customizable forms with Superform in Rails that permit their own parameters, making form building faster and easier. Customize forms with Phlex components.

recent_posts.title: Sqlite & Rails in Production
recent_posts.summary: Sqlite and Litestack run as separate processes that need to be monitored. Usually these processes are running on a separate server that’s accessed over a network connection, which can also break. You’ll either have to deal with that complexity yourself or pay to have it managed with services like Upstash Redis.
